lessons.title: Handling errors
lessons.summary: try and except, catching the right error, else and finally, and raising your own.

sections.heading: Errors you expect
sections.body:
Some errors aren't bugs; they're things that can genuinely happen. A user types `ten` when you asked for a number. A file isn't where it should be. Instead of letting the program crash, you can **handle** the error with `try` and `except`.

Python runs the `try` block. If an error happens inside it, Python jumps straight to the matching `except` block instead of crashing. If no error happens, the except block is skipped.

example.explain: int("ten") raises a ValueError, so `Got` never prints and the except block runs.

sections.heading: Catch the specific error
sections.body:
Always name the error type you expect, like `except ValueError:`. A bare `except:` catches **everything**, including typos in your own code (a NameError) and even Ctrl+C, which hides real bugs. You can catch several types with `except (ValueError, ZeroDivisionError):`, and get the error's message with `except ValueError as error:`.

Keep the try block small: just the line that might fail. The less it contains, the less chance of catching something you didn't mean to.

sections.heading: else and finally
sections.body: An `else:` block after the excepts runs only if **no** error happened, which keeps the try block small. A `finally:` block runs **no matter what**, error or not, which is used for clean-up like closing things.

sections.heading: Raising errors
sections.body: Your own functions can raise errors with `raise`, to refuse bad input loudly rather than return a wrong answer. Pick a fitting built-in type: `ValueError` for a bad value, `TypeError` for a wrong type. Whoever calls your function can catch it.

key_points: `try:` runs code; `except SomeError:` runs if that error happens.
Name the specific error. Bare `except:` hides bugs.
`else` runs when nothing failed; `finally` always runs.
`raise ValueError("message")` refuses bad input from your own functions.
mistakes: Using bare `except:` and silently hiding a typo.
Wrapping the whole program in one giant try.
Returning a made-up value like -1 instead of raising an error.
lessons.try_it: Write a loop that keeps asking for a number with `input()` until it gets a valid one, using try and except ValueError. Write a function that raises ValueError for negative ages and call it inside try.

quiz.question: What does `try: int("x")` / `except ValueError: print("bad")` print?
quiz.explain: int("x") raises ValueError, which the except catches.

quiz.question: Why avoid a bare `except:`?
choices: It catches every error, hiding real bugs
quiz.explain: It catches everything, including mistakes in your own code that you'd want to see.

quiz.question: When does a `finally` block run?
choices: Only if there was an error
quiz.explain: finally runs whether or not an error happened.

lessons.title: Reading and writing files
lessons.summary: Opening files with with, reading lines, writing and appending, and paths.

sections.heading: Opening a file
sections.body:
`open(path, mode)` opens a file. The mode says what you'll do: `"r"` read (the default), `"w"` write (which **empties the file first**, or creates it), and `"a"` append (adds to the end). Text files should also say their encoding, `encoding="utf-8"`, so special characters like £ work everywhere.

Always open files with a `with` block. When the block ends, Python closes the file for you, even if an error happened inside. Forgetting to close files can lose data that hadn't been written yet.

example.code:
with open("orders.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("margherita\n")
    file.write("pepperoni\n")

with open("orders.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.strip())
example.explain: write doesn't add new lines for you, so include `\n`. Looping over a file gives one line at a time, each ending in `\n`, which strip removes.

sections.heading: Reading all at once
sections.body:
`file.read()` gives the whole file as one string. `file.read().splitlines()` gives a list of lines without the `\n`s, which is often the most convenient form.

If the file doesn't exist, opening it for reading raises `FileNotFoundError`, which you can catch with try/except.

sections.heading: Paths
sections.body: A path like `"orders.txt"` is **relative**: it means "in the current folder", which is wherever the program was started from, not necessarily where the script lives. The `pathlib` module makes paths easier: `Path.home() / "notes.txt"` builds a path in your home folder, and `Path("orders.txt").read_text()` reads a whole file in one call.

example.code:
from pathlib import Path

notes = Path("notes.txt")
notes.write_text("Buy flour\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(notes.exists(), notes.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip())

key_points: Use `with open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8") as file:` so files always close.
`"w"` empties the file first; `"a"` appends; `"r"` reads.
Looping over a file gives lines with `\n`; strip them.
`pathlib.Path` makes building and reading paths simpler.
mistakes: Opening with `"w"` when you meant `"a"`, wiping the file.
Forgetting `\n` when writing lines, so everything ends up on one line.
Assuming the current folder is the script's folder.
lessons.try_it: Write a script that appends whatever you type into `input()` to a file called `log.txt`, then prints every line in the file with a line number.

quiz.question: What does opening an existing file with mode `"w"` do?
quiz.explain: w truncates the file to nothing before you write.

quiz.question: Why use `with open(...) as file:`?
choices: It closes the file automatically, even after an error
It's the only way to read
quiz.explain: The with block guarantees the file is closed when it ends.

quiz.question: What does `file.write("hi")` add?
quiz.explain: write adds exactly the text given. Add `\n` yourself for a new line.

lessons.title: Classes and objects
lessons.summary: Making your own types: __init__, attributes, methods, self and __str__.

sections.heading: Bundling data with behaviour
sections.body:
A **class** is a blueprint for making your own kind of value. Each value made from it is an **object** (or **instance**). Objects hold their own data, in **attributes**, and have their own functions, called **methods**. You've used plenty already: every string is an object of class `str`, and `.upper()` is one of its methods.

Classes are useful when several values belong together and some functions only make sense on them: an order has items, a customer and a status, and you can add an item to it or work out its total.

sections.heading: __init__ and self
sections.body:
`__init__` is a special method that runs when you create an object, to set up its attributes. Its first parameter, `self`, is the object being created. Inside any method, `self` is the object the method was called on, and `self.name = value` stores an attribute on it.

You create an object by calling the class like a function: `Order("Ana")`. Python makes a new object and passes it to `__init__` as `self`, along with your arguments. You never pass `self` yourself.

example.explain: Prints `Ana 2 10.0`. Each Order has its own list of items.

sections.heading: __str__ and good design
sections.body:
`__str__` is another special method: it returns the text shown when the object is printed or put in an f-string. Without it, printing shows something like `<__main__.Order object at 0x7f...>`.

Good methods keep the object's data valid. Rather than letting other code change `order.items` directly in strange ways, provide methods like `add` and `remove` that check their input, and raise errors when something isn't allowed.

key_points: A class is a blueprint; calling it makes an object.
Methods take `self` first; call them as `obj.method(args)`.
mistakes: Forgetting `self` as a method's first parameter.
Writing `items = []` instead of `self.items = []` in `__init__`, so it's lost.
Defining a list as a class-level attribute, which every object then shares.
lessons.try_it: Write a `Counter` class with a `count` attribute starting at 0, an `increase(amount=1)` method, a `reset()` method and a `__str__`. Make two counters and show they count separately.

quiz.question: What is `self` inside a method?
choices: The object the method was called on
A keyword you must type in calls
quiz.explain: self is the particular object, so each object keeps its own attributes.

quiz.question: What runs when you write `Order("Ana")`?
choices: Nothing until you call a method
quiz.explain: Creating an object calls __init__ to set it up.

quiz.question: What does `__str__` decide?
quiz.explain: print and f-strings use the text __str__ returns.

lessons.title: Modules and the standard library
lessons.summary: import, from, writing your own modules, and the most useful built-in modules.

sections.heading: import
sections.body:
A **module** is a file of Python code you can use from another file. `import math` gives you the `math` module, and you use what's inside with a dot: `math.sqrt(16)`. `from math import sqrt, pi` brings specific names in directly, so you can write `sqrt(16)`.

Any `.py` file is a module. If you have `prices.py` in the same folder, `import prices` lets you use its functions as `prices.pizza_price(...)`.

sections.heading: if __name__ == "__main__"
sections.body: When a file is imported, all of its top-level code runs. That's a problem if it also has code that reads input or prints. The fix is a special check: code inside `if __name__ == "__main__":` runs only when the file is run directly, not when it's imported. It's how you write a file that's both a useful module and a runnable program.

sections.heading: The standard library
sections.body: Python comes with a huge **standard library**, so you rarely start from scratch. Some you'll use often:

example.code:
import json
import random
from collections import Counter

print(random.choice(["ham", "olives", "peppers"]))
print(Counter("pepperoni").most_common(1))
print(json.dumps({"pizza": "veggie", "slices": 8}))

bullets: `json`: turn dicts and lists into text and back (`json.dumps`, `json.loads`), for saving data and talking to websites.
`collections.Counter`: the counting pattern, done for you.

sections.heading: Installing more
sections.body: Beyond the standard library, thousands of packages exist on PyPI, installed with `pip`. On Arch, prefer `sudo pacman -S python-<name>` where a package exists, or create a **virtual environment** for each project with `python3 -m venv .venv`, so projects don't interfere with each other or with the system.

key_points: `import module` then `module.name`; `from module import name` for direct use.
Any .py file is a module you can import.
Put a program's top-level actions under `if __name__ == "__main__":`.
Check the standard library (math, random, json, datetime, collections) before writing your own.
mistakes: Naming your own file `random.py` or `json.py`, which hides the real module.
Top-level prints in a module that run every time it's imported.
Installing packages system-wide with pip instead of using pacman or a venv.
lessons.try_it: In the prompt, try `import random` and roll a die ten times. Use `collections.Counter` to count the letters in a sentence. Turn a dictionary into JSON text and back with `json.dumps` and `json.loads`.

quiz.question: After `from math import sqrt`, how do you call it?
quiz.explain: from-import brings the name in directly.

quiz.question: What does `if __name__ == "__main__":` protect?
choices: Code that should only run when the file is run directly, not imported
quiz.explain: When imported, __name__ is the module's name, so the block is skipped.

quiz.question: Why is naming your script `random.py` a problem?
choices: `import random` would find your file instead of the real module
quiz.explain: Python looks in the script's folder first, so your file hides the standard one.
